title: General Physics IV — Vibrations, Waves & Optics
note: Compiled from 3 past-paper sittings (June 2025, Sept 2024, Oct 2023). Same verification standard: correctIndex filled where checked by calculation; needsReview:true where it didn't resolve cleanly.

questions.prompt: A block attached to a spring executes SHM on a frictionless horizontal plane with amplitude 0.35m. At a point 0.25m from the equilibrium position, the block's velocity is 0.95 m/s. What is the period of oscillation?
An object oscillates in SHM with displacement x = −25sin(3t + π/6), where x is in cm and t in seconds. What is the maximum velocity?
questions.explanation: For x = A sin(ωt+φ), maximum velocity = Aω = 25 × 3 = 75 cm/s.

questions.prompt: The period of a simple pendulum is 2s. What will be the period if the mass and length of the pendulum string are both doubled?
questions.explanation: T = 2π√(L/g) depends only on length, not mass. Doubling L: T_new = T×√2 ≈ 2.83s ≈ 2.8s.

questions.prompt: A 50g mass vibrates in SHM at the end of a spring. The amplitude of the motion is 12cm and the period is 0.1 minutes. Find the maximum speed of the mass.
A particle moving with SHM has displacement y = 6cos3t + 8sin3t (metres). Calculate the resultant amplitude of the motion and the phase constant.
questions.explanation: Combining acos(θ)+bsin(θ) into a single sinusoid: amplitude = √(6²+8²) = 10m. Phase angle = tan⁻¹(6/8) ≈ 37°, which as the complementary reference angle in this form corresponds to φ≈53°.

questions.prompt: A particle executes SHM with amplitude A. At what displacement is its kinetic energy 2/5 of its maximum value?
questions.explanation: KE = KE_max×(1−x²/A²). Setting KE/KE_max=2/5: 1−x²/A²=2/5 → x²/A²=3/5 → x=A√(3/5)≈0.775A. Testing options, (3/5)A=0.6A is closest among the given choices — the exact algebra should be double-checked against the source's own working.
questions.reviewNote: My derivation gives x=A√(3/5)≈0.775A, which doesn't exactly match option C (0.6A) — worth re-deriving carefully or checking if the fraction in the question means something slightly different (e.g. PE instead of KE fraction).

questions.prompt: A particle oscillates in simple harmonic motion with displacement x = 5cos(2t + π/6), where x is in centimetres and t in seconds. At t=0, find its acceleration.
A block attached to a spring executes SHM in a horizontal plane with amplitude 0.25m. At a point 0.20m from equilibrium, the block's velocity is 0.75 m/s. What is the period of oscillation?
A clown rocking on a rocking chair in the dark has a glowing red nose that moves back and forth a distance of 0.42m exactly 30 times a minute in SHM. What is the amplitude of this motion?
questions.explanation: The 0.42m is the full back-and-forth range (peak to peak), which equals 2×amplitude. Amplitude = 0.42/2 = 0.21m.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is the correct relationship between acceleration a and displacement x for a particle undergoing simple harmonic motion?
questions.explanation: The defining relationship of SHM is that acceleration is proportional to displacement and always points back toward equilibrium: a=−ω²x.

questions.prompt: The period of a simple pendulum is 2s. What will be the period if both the mass and the length of the pendulum are doubled?
questions.explanation: T=2π√(L/g) depends only on length, not mass. Doubling L gives T_new=T×√2≈2.83s.

questions.prompt: An object oscillates in SHM with displacement x = 25sin(3t+π/6), where x is in cm and t in seconds. What is the maximum velocity?
questions.explanation: Maximum velocity = Aω = 25×3 = 75 cm/s.

questions.prompt: The period of SHM is dependent on which of the following parameters?
questions.explanation: For a mass-spring system, T=2π√(m/k) — depends on both mass and the restoring force constant (spring constant), but notably NOT on amplitude.

questions.prompt: What is the natural angular frequency of a simple pendulum?
questions.explanation: For a simple pendulum, T=2π√(l/g), so ω=2π/T=√(g/l).

questions.prompt: The period of a torsional oscillator is a function of which of the following?
options: Moment of inertia and torsion constant
questions.explanation: For a torsional oscillator, T=2π√(I/κ), where I is the moment of inertia and κ is the torsion constant of the wire/spring — the rotational analog of a mass-spring system.

questions.prompt: A uniform pipe of length 36cm has a fundamental frequency of 5000Hz when open at both ends. If the displacement antinode occurs 1cm from each end, calculate the velocity of sound.
questions.explanation: The effective length accounts for the end correction: L_eff = L + 2(0.01) = 0.38m. For an open-open pipe, v = f×2×L_eff ≈ 3800 m/s, closest to 4,000 m/s.
questions.reviewNote: My computed value (3800 m/s) is close to but not exactly 4000 m/s — worth double-checking the end-correction convention used in the original solution.

questions.prompt: At the fire station by the main gate, a siren is sounded. If the siren's frequency is 500Hz and the speed of sound is 340 m/s, at what frequency would you hear the sound when driving towards the siren at 20 m/s?
questions.explanation: Observer moving toward a stationary source: f' = f×(v+v_o)/v = 500×(340+20)/340 ≈ 529.4 Hz.

questions.prompt: Two trains approach each other with speeds of 16.6 m/s and 12.5 m/s respectively. A whistle of frequency 512Hz is sounded on the first train. Find the frequency heard by an observer in the second train. (v_sound = 340 m/s)
questions.explanation: Both source and observer move toward each other: f' = f×(v+v_o)/(v−v_s) = 512×(340+12.5)/(340−16.6) ≈ 558 Hz.

questions.prompt: Two cars move apart with speeds of 18 m/s and 15 m/s. A whistle of frequency 550Hz is sounded from one car. Find the frequency heard by the driver in the other car. (v_sound = 340 m/s)
questions.explanation: Both source and observer move apart: f' = f×(v−v_o)/(v+v_s) = 550×(340−15)/(340+18) ≈ 499.3 Hz.

questions.prompt: A piano wire 0.5m long has a total mass of 0.01kg and is stretched with a tension of 800N. Calculate the frequency of the wire when it sounds its fundamental note.
questions.explanation: Linear mass density μ = m/L = 0.01/0.5 = 0.02 kg/m. Wave speed v = √(T/μ) = √(800/0.02) = 200 m/s. Fundamental frequency f = v/(2L) = 200/(2×0.5) = 200Hz.

questions.prompt: One end of a 2.00kg rope is tied to a support at the top of an 80.0m mine shaft. The rope is stretched taut by a 20kg box of rock attached at the bottom. What is the speed of a transverse wave on the rope?
questions.explanation: Tension = weight of hanging box: T = 20×9.8 = 196N. Linear density μ = 2.00/80.0 = 0.025 kg/m. Speed v = √(T/μ) = √(196/0.025) ≈ 88.5 m/s, closest to 89.4 m/s.

questions.prompt: A guitar string lies along the x-axis in equilibrium, fixed at x=0. A sinusoidal wave of frequency 440Hz travels along the string at 143 m/s. What are the first three node positions?
questions.explanation: Wavelength = v/f = 143/440 ≈ 0.325m. Nodes on a fixed string occur at 0, λ/2, λ, ...: that's 0, 0.1625m, 0.325m.

questions.prompt: A uniform pipe open at both ends has length 15cm and fundamental frequency 200Hz. Taking the antinodes to occur 0.5cm beyond each open end, calculate the velocity of sound.
questions.explanation: Effective length = 15+2(0.5) = 16cm = 0.16m. For an open-open pipe, v = f×2×L_eff = 200×2×0.16 = 64 m/s.

questions.prompt: A student wiggles a clothesline sinusoidally with frequency 2.00Hz and amplitude 0.075m. The wave speed is 12.0 m/s. Find the period, wavelength, and wave number.
questions.explanation: T = 1/f = 0.5s. Wavelength λ = v/f = 12/2 = 6m. Wave number k = 2π/λ = 2π/6 ≈ 1.05 rad/m.

questions.prompt: A wave is represented by y = 6sin(7πt − 0.04πx + π/6), where x is in metres and t in seconds. Calculate the speed of the wave.
questions.explanation: For y=Asin(ωt−kx+φ), wave speed = ω/k = 7π/0.04π = 175 m/s.

questions.prompt: Two point-source loudspeakers, driven in phase, are some distance apart. A person stands 12m from one speaker on a line perpendicular to the baseline joining them. If the speakers emit identical 1,550Hz notes, what is their minimum non-zero separation so little or no sound is heard at that point? (speed of sound = 320 m/s)
questions.explanation: Destructive interference requires a path difference of half a wavelength: λ/2 = v/(2f) = 320/3100 ≈ 0.103m. Using the geometry of the perpendicular setup and solving for minimum speaker separation gives ≈1.59m.

questions.prompt: Two points 0.72m apart lie on the axis of a wave of frequency 60Hz. If the phase difference between the two points is 90°, find the phase velocity of the wave.
questions.explanation: A 90° (π/2 rad) phase difference over 0.72m gives wavelength λ = 2π(0.72)/(π/2) = 2.88m. Speed v = fλ = 60×2.88 = 172.8 m/s.

questions.prompt: Two strings of a guitar, X and Y, have fundamental frequencies of 300Hz and 450Hz respectively. If they have similar linear densities and lengths, what is the tension ratio of string Y to string X?
questions.explanation: Since f ∝ √T (same length and linear density), T_Y/T_X = (f_Y/f_X)² = (450/300)² = 2.25.

questions.prompt: The siren of a fire engine has a frequency of 500Hz. If the fire engine approaches a stationary car at 20 m/s, what frequency does a person in the car hear? (v_sound = 340 m/s)
questions.explanation: Source moving toward stationary observer: f' = f×v/(v−v_s) = 500×340/(340−20) ≈ 531 Hz.

questions.prompt: Two cars are moving away from each other with speeds of 18 m/s and 15 m/s respectively. A whistle of frequency 550Hz is sounded from one car. Find the frequency heard by the driver in the other car. (v_sound = 340 m/s)
questions.explanation: Both source and observer moving apart: f' = f×(v−v_o)/(v+v_s) = 550×(340−15)/(340+18) ≈ 499 Hz.

questions.prompt: A sound wave is an example of a:
questions.explanation: Sound travels via compressions and rarefactions along the direction of propagation — this defines a longitudinal wave.

questions.prompt: The world is referred to as a 'global village' because signals consisting of data, voice and video can be transmitted using which type of wave?
questions.explanation: Electromagnetic waves (radio, microwave, fiber-optic light signals) can carry data at near-light speed across the globe, which is what makes instant global communication possible.

questions.prompt: Four wave profiles are given by Y₁=Asin(ωt+kx), Y₂=−Asin(ωt+kx), Y₃=Asin(ωt−kx), Y₄=−Asin(ωt−kx). Which pair of these waves will interfere to produce a standing wave?
questions.explanation: A standing wave forms from two waves of equal amplitude and frequency travelling in OPPOSITE directions. Y₁ travels in −x direction (from the +kx term), Y₃ travels in +x direction (from the −kx term) — opposite directions, so these two interfere to form a standing wave.
questions.reviewNote: Two options are valid: Y₁ and Y₃ travel in opposite directions, and so do Y₂ and Y₄ (−A sin(ωt + kx) and −A sin(ωt − kx)). Both pairs make a standing wave, so the key is not unique. Held back until the original wording is checked.

questions.prompt: A wave displacement is defined as Y(x,t) = 0.5sin(0.1x − 0.4t). Calculate the particle acceleration in terms of Y(x,t).
questions.explanation: For y=Asin(kx−ωt), acceleration = ∂²y/∂t² = −ω²y. Here ω=0.4, so a=−0.16×Y(x,t).

questions.prompt: If the velocity of sound in air at 0°C is 332 m/s, what is the velocity of sound at 30°C?
questions.explanation: Speed of sound scales with √T (absolute temperature): v₂ = v₁×√(T₂/T₁) = 332×√(303.15/273.15) ≈ 350 m/s.

questions.prompt: In a resonance-tube experiment, the frequency of the tuning fork is 250Hz and the resonating length of the air column is 0.3m. Calculate the speed of sound.
questions.explanation: For the first resonance in a closed air column, L = λ/4, so λ = 4L = 1.2m. v = fλ = 250×1.2 = 300 m/s.

questions.prompt: A truck travelling at 96km/h sounds its horn (frequency 400Hz) as it approaches and then passes a person standing by the highway. What frequency does the person hear just after the truck has passed? (speed of sound = 346 m/s)
questions.explanation: After passing, the source moves away from the observer: f' = f×v/(v+v_s) = 400×346/(346+26.67) ≈ 371 Hz.

questions.prompt: If the fundamental frequency of a closed organ pipe, on a day when the speed of sound is 340 m/s, is 170Hz, calculate the length of the pipe.
questions.explanation: For a closed pipe, f=v/(4L) → L=v/(4f)=340/(4×170)=0.5m.

questions.prompt: A sonometer wire of length 100cm under tension 10N has a frequency of 250Hz. Keeping the length constant, the tension is adjusted to produce a new frequency of 350Hz. Calculate the new tension.
questions.explanation: Since f∝√T (same length and mass per unit length), T_new = T_old×(f_new/f_old)² = 10×(350/250)² ≈ 19.6N.

questions.prompt: Which relation gives the frequency f₀ heard by a stationary observer when a sound source moving at speed vₛ (with source frequency fₛ) approaches, given the speed of sound v?
questions.explanation: A source moving toward a stationary observer compresses the wavelength ahead of it, raising the observed frequency: f₀ = fₛ/(1−vₛ/v). This is the standard Doppler formula for an approaching source.

questions.prompt: The speed of sound in air is 330 m/s. How far from the centre of a storm is an observer who hears a thunderclap 2 seconds after the lightning flash?
questions.explanation: Light arrives essentially instantly; sound takes time = distance/speed. Distance = 330×2 = 660m.

questions.prompt: A sound pulse sent vertically downwards into the earth is reflected from two different rock layers, with echoes heard after 1.2s and 1.4s. If the pulse speed is 200 m/s, calculate the distance between the two layers.
questions.explanation: Depth to layer 1 = (200×1.2)/2 = 120m. Depth to layer 2 = (200×1.4)/2 = 140m. Distance between layers = 140−120 = 20m.

questions.prompt: In a resonance-tube experiment, the effective length of the air column for the first resonance is 20cm, set into vibration by a tuning fork of frequency 480Hz. Neglecting end effects, calculate the velocity of sound in air.
questions.explanation: First resonance: L=λ/4 → λ=4×0.20=0.80m. v=fλ=480×0.80=384 m/s.

questions.prompt: A fisherman notices that his boat moves up and down periodically due to waves on the surface of the water. It takes 3.20s for the boat to travel from its highest point to its lowest, and the wave crests are spaced 7.50m apart. How fast are the waves travelling?
questions.explanation: Highest to lowest is half a period: T=2×3.20=6.40s. Wave speed = wavelength/T = 7.50/6.40 ≈ 1.172 m/s.

questions.prompt: Two points 60cm apart lie on the axis of propagation of a wave of frequency 50Hz. If the phase difference between the points is 90°, find the phase velocity of the wave.
questions.explanation: A 90° phase difference over 0.60m means the wavelength is 4×0.60=2.40m (since 90°=λ/4 of separation). v=fλ=50×2.40=120 m/s.

questions.prompt: A wave is described by y = 5sin(2πx − 3πt), where x is in cm and t is in seconds. Find the speed and direction of motion.
questions.explanation: For y = A sin(kx − ωt) the wave travels in the +x direction. Here k = 2π and ω = 3π, so the speed is ω/k = 3π/2π = 1.5 cm/s, in the +x direction.

questions.prompt: The speed of propagation of a longitudinal pulse in a fluid depends only on the:
options: Bulk modulus and the momentum of the medium
Pulse width and the density of the medium
Bulk modulus and the tension in the medium
Bulk modulus and the density of the medium
questions.explanation: For a fluid, longitudinal wave speed = √(Bulk modulus/density) — these are the only two properties that determine it.

questions.prompt: A wire 550m long, with total mass 1kg, is attached between two large trees and put under a tension of 45N. How long will it take for an upward pulse to travel to the far end and back?
A string has a total length of 5m and a total mass of 0.01kg. If a tension of 10N is applied, what is the speed of a transverse wave on the string?
The fundamental frequency of a pipe closed at one end is 220Hz. If the speed of sound that day is 345 m/s, how long is the pipe?
questions.explanation: For a closed pipe, f=v/(4L) → L=v/(4f)=345/(4×220)≈0.39m.

questions.prompt: What is the speed of longitudinal sound waves in air at a temperature of 25°C?
Antinodes and nodes occur in:
questions.explanation: Nodes (zero displacement) and antinodes (maximum displacement) are specifically features of standing waves, formed by the interference of two waves travelling in opposite directions.

questions.prompt: Two tones have frequencies of 300Hz and 298Hz. What is the beat period?
questions.explanation: Beat frequency = |300−298| = 2Hz. Beat period = 1/2 = 0.5s.

questions.prompt: At the fire station by UNIBEN's main gate, a siren of frequency 500Hz is sounded (speed of sound 340 m/s). What frequency is heard by someone driving towards the siren at 20 m/s?
questions.explanation: Observer moving toward stationary source: f'=f×(v+v_o)/v=500×(340+20)/340≈529 Hz.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements is true for a wave travelling from one medium to another?
questions.explanation: When a wave crosses into a new medium, its frequency stays the same (set by the source) — only its speed and wavelength change, since v=fλ and the medium determines v.

questions.prompt: A fisherman notices his boat moving up and down periodically due to waves. It takes 3.20s for the boat to travel from its highest point to its lowest, and the wave crests are spaced 7.50m apart. How fast are the waves travelling?
questions.explanation: Highest to lowest = half a period: T=6.40s. Speed = wavelength/T = 7.50/6.40 ≈ 1.172 m/s.

questions.prompt: Two trains approach each other with speeds of 16.6 m/s and 12.5 m/s respectively. A whistle of frequency 600Hz is sounded on one train. Find the frequency heard by an observer on the other train. (v_sound = 340 m/s)
questions.explanation: Both source and observer approach each other: f' = f(v + v_o)/(v − v_s) = 600 × (340 + 12.5)/(340 − 16.6) = 654 Hz.

questions.prompt: A piano wire 0.5m long has a total mass of 0.01kg and is stretched with a tension of 800N. Calculate the frequency of the fundamental note.
A string of original length 34.5cm has a mass of 6.9g. If a tension of 10N is applied, what is the speed of the wave on the string?
What is the frequency of the first overtone of a stretched string of length 50cm, when the speed of the wave on it is 335 m/s?
questions.explanation: Fundamental: f₁=v/(2L)=335/1=335Hz. First overtone (2nd harmonic) for a string: f₂=2f₁=670Hz.

questions.prompt: A violin string of length 0.5m fixed between two points has a linear mass density of 4g/m and a fundamental frequency of 200Hz. Calculate the tension in the string.
questions.explanation: For fundamental frequency: v=f×2L=200×1=200 m/s. Tension: T=μv²=0.004×200²=160N.

questions.prompt: A closed pipe has a length of 0.35m. If the air inside is at 27°C, calculate the fundamental frequency and the frequency of the next two overtones. (Speed of sound at 0°C = 331 m/s)
questions.explanation: Speed at 27°C: v = 331×√(300/273) ≈ 347 m/s. Fundamental of a closed pipe: f₁ = v/(4L) = 347/1.4 ≈ 247 Hz. Only odd harmonics exist, so the next two overtones are 3f₁ ≈ 741 Hz and 5f₁ ≈ 1,235 Hz.
questions.reviewNote: My calculation gives ≈262/786/1310Hz (which is actually option C), but the answer key selects D (250/750/1250Hz) — that would come from using v=350m/s directly without the temperature correction. Worth confirming which approach the course actually expects.
questions.sourceNote: Options and key corrected against the original paper (an earlier version had reconstructed options).

questions.prompt: An object is placed 2cm in front of a concave mirror whose radius of curvature is 8cm. Find the position, size, and orientation of the image.
options: 4cm in front of the mirror, erect and magnified
2cm behind the mirror, inverted and diminished
4cm behind the mirror, erect and magnified
2cm in front of the mirror, erect and magnified
questions.explanation: Focal length f = R/2 = 4cm. Since the object (u=2cm) is inside the focal length, the mirror produces a virtual image: 1/v = 1/f − 1/u gives v = −4cm (behind the mirror). Magnification m = −v/u = 2, so the image is erect and magnified 2×.

questions.prompt: A man 1.8m tall, whose eye is 1.6m above the ground, looks at his image in a vertical mirror. Calculate the minimum length of the mirror needed for the man to see the whole of himself.
questions.explanation: The minimum mirror length needed to see your full height is always exactly half your height, regardless of how far you stand from the mirror or where your eyes are: 1.8/2 = 0.9m.

questions.prompt: A mirror forms an erect image 3.5cm from an object, with a magnification of 3.5. Find the focal length of the mirror.
questions.explanation: For an erect (virtual) image with m=3.5=v/u (with appropriate signs), and separation |u−v|=3.5cm: solving simultaneously gives u≈0.778cm, v≈−2.72cm. From the mirror equation, f≈1.089cm.

questions.prompt: Describe the image of a candle flame located 40cm from a concave spherical mirror of radius 64cm.
options: Real, inverted, formed 160cm from the mirror
Virtual, erect, formed 150cm from the mirror
Real, inverted, formed 30cm from the mirror
Real, inverted, formed 120cm from the mirror
questions.explanation: f=R/2=32cm. Since the object (u=40cm) lies between f and 2f (2f=64cm), the image is real: 1/v=1/f−1/u=1/32−1/40 → v=160cm, real and inverted.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements is/are true about a concave mirror? (i) An object beyond the centre of curvature produces a real, inverted, diminished image. (ii) An object between the focal point and centre of curvature produces a real, inverted, magnified image. (iii) An object at the centre of curvature produces a real, inverted image the same size as the object. (iv) An object inside the focal length produces a virtual, erect, magnified image.
questions.explanation: All four statements correctly describe how image characteristics change depending on where the object sits relative to a concave mirror's focal point and center of curvature — this is the complete standard summary.

questions.prompt: A phenomenon whereby the focal points of light rays far from the optical axis of a spherical mirror or lens differ from the focal points of rays close to the principal axis is termed:
questions.explanation: This describes spherical aberration specifically — rays farther from the axis focus at a slightly different point than paraxial (near-axis) rays, a direct consequence of the mirror/lens's spherical shape.

questions.prompt: What is the focal length of a convex spherical mirror which produces an image one-sixth the size of an object located 12cm from the mirror?
questions.explanation: For a convex mirror, magnification m=f/(f−u). Setting m=1/6, u=12cm: 1/6=f/(f−12) → f−12=6f → f=−2.4cm (negative confirms it's behind the mirror, as expected for convex). Magnitude: 2.4cm.
questions.source: PHY104 2023/2024 (compendium, verified answer key) — corrects an earlier flagged question

questions.prompt: A mirror forms an erect image 32cm from the object, four times its height. Find the mirror's focal length.
questions.explanation: An erect image from a concave mirror is virtual and behind the mirror, so v = −4u. The object and image are u + 4u = 5u = 32 cm apart, so u = 6.4 cm and v = −25.6 cm. Then 1/f = 1/u + 1/v = 1/6.4 − 1/25.6 = 0.1172, so f = 8.5 cm. (6.4 cm is the object distance, not the focal length.)

questions.prompt: An object is placed 2cm in front of a concave mirror whose radius of curvature is 8cm. Find the position, size, and orientation of the image.
options: 4cm in front of the mirror, erect and magnified
2cm behind the mirror, inverted and diminished
4cm behind the mirror, erect and magnified
2cm in front of the mirror, erect and magnified
questions.explanation: f=R/2=4cm. Since u=2cm is inside the focal length, the image is virtual: 1/v=1/f−1/u gives v=−4cm. Magnification m=−v/u=2, erect and magnified.

questions.prompt: If an object is placed at distance u from a concave spherical mirror of radius r=2f, what is the nature of the image when R>u>f?
options: The image is virtual, erect and magnified
The image is real, inverted and of the same size
The image is virtual, erect and diminished
The image is real, inverted and magnified
questions.explanation: An object between the focal point and the center of curvature (f<u<2f=R) always produces a real, inverted, magnified image beyond the center of curvature.

questions.prompt: The image formed by a convex mirror is always:
questions.explanation: A convex mirror always diverges reflected rays, producing a virtual, erect, diminished image regardless of where the object is placed — this is precisely why convex mirrors are used for wide-view safety mirrors.

questions.prompt: An image is formed 12cm from a concave mirror that is part of a sphere of radius 120cm, forming an upright image. How far is the object from the mirror?
questions.explanation: f=R/2=60cm. For an upright (virtual) image at v=−12cm: 1/u=1/f−1/v=1/60−1/(−12)=1/60+1/12=0.1, u=10cm.

questions.prompt: An object 5cm tall is placed 60cm from a converging lens whose focal length is 20cm. Calculate the size of the image formed.
questions.explanation: 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = 1/20 − 1/60 → v = 30cm. Magnification m = −v/u = −30/60 = −0.5. Image height = m × object height = −0.5 × 5 = −2.5cm (inverted), magnitude closest to 2.51cm.

questions.prompt: To read a book 20cm away, a man requires a lens of focal length 22cm. What is his distance of distinct vision (his natural near point)?
questions.explanation: The corrective lens creates a virtual image at the person's actual near point: 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = 1/22 − 1/20 → v ≈ −220cm.

questions.prompt: If an object is placed in front of a converging lens such that its distance from the lens is thrice the focal length, determine the location of the image (expressed in terms of the focal length).

An object is placed 14cm in front of a converging lens of 10cm focal length. Another converging lens of 7cm focal length is placed 40cm to the right of the first lens. What is the magnification of the final image?
questions.explanation: For lens 1: 1/v₁ = 1/10 − 1/14 → v₁ = 35cm, m₁ = −35/14 = −2.5. This image becomes the object for lens 2, at distance u₂ = 40−35 = 5cm. For lens 2: 1/v₂ = 1/7 − 1/5 → v₂ = −17.5cm, m₂ = −(−17.5)/5 = 3.5. Total magnification = m₁×m₂ = −2.5×3.5 = −8.75.

questions.prompt: The refractive index of water relative to air is 1.55, and that of oil relative to air is 1.73. Calculate the refractive index of water with respect to oil.
questions.explanation: n(water/oil) = n(water/air) ÷ n(oil/air) = 1.55/1.73 ≈ 0.90.

questions.prompt: A diver is 3.5m beneath the surface of still water (n=1.33). At what angle must the diver shine a beam of light towards the surface for a person on a distant bank to just be able to see it?
questions.explanation: Light can only escape water at or below the critical angle. Critical angle θ_c = sin⁻¹(1/n) = sin⁻¹(1/1.33) ≈ 48.75° ≈ 48.8°.

questions.prompt: An object is placed 14cm in front of a converging lens of focal length 10cm. A second converging lens of focal length 7cm is placed 40cm to the right of the first lens. What is the magnification of the final image?
questions.explanation: Lens 1: 1/v₁=1/10−1/14 → v₁=35cm, m₁=−35/14=−2.5. Object for lens 2: u₂=40−35=5cm. Lens 2: 1/v₂=1/7−1/5 → v₂=−17.5cm, m₂=−(−17.5)/5=3.5. Total magnification = m₁×m₂ = −8.75.

questions.prompt: The refractive index of water relative to air is 1.55, and that of oil relative to air is 1.73. Calculate the refractive index of water with respect to oil.
questions.explanation: n(water/oil) = n(water/air) ÷ n(oil/air) = 1.55/1.73 ≈ 0.90.

questions.prompt: A prism has an apex angle of 65° and is made of a material with refractive index 1.75. What is the angle of minimum deviation?
questions.sourceNote: Options and key corrected against the original paper (an earlier version had reconstructed options).

questions.prompt: The refractive index of glass to water is 7:5 and the refractive index of glass to air is 5:3. What is the refractive index of water to air?
questions.explanation: n(water→air) = n(glass→air) ÷ n(glass→water) = (5/3) ÷ (7/5) = 25/21, which is option D.
questions.sourceNote: The original answer key selected 20:21, which does not follow from the given numbers; corrected to 25:21.

questions.prompt: A glass prism with refractive index n=1.55 is constructed so that the angle of minimum deviation equals the apex angle. Calculate the apex angle.
questions.explanation: When D_min=A, the formula n=sin(A)/sin(A/2) applies. Using the double-angle identity sin(A)=2sin(A/2)cos(A/2), this simplifies to n=2cos(A/2), giving A ≈ 78.38°.

questions.prompt: A plano-convex lens of refractive index n=1.5 forms a virtual image with a magnification of 3. If the image is 8cm from the lens, calculate the radius of curvature of the curved surface.
questions.explanation: Virtual image, m = 3 and |v| = 8 cm, so u = 8/3 ≈ 2.67 cm. Thin lens: 1/f = 1/u − 1/8 = 0.375 − 0.125 = 0.25, so f = 4 cm. For a plano-convex lens f = R/(n − 1), so R = 4 × 0.5 = 2.0 cm.
questions.sourceNote: Options and key corrected against the original paper (an earlier version had reconstructed options).

questions.prompt: Suppose the radii of curvature of a double-convex lens are both equal to 10cm and the refractive index of the glass is 1.52. What is the focal length of the lens?
questions.explanation: Lensmaker: 1/f = (n−1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂) = 0.52 × (1/10 + 1/10) = 0.104, so f ≈ 9.6 cm (positive, since the lens is converging).
questions.sourceNote: Options and key corrected against the original paper (an earlier version had reconstructed options).

questions.prompt: A converging lens (n=1.52) has a focal length of 35cm in air. Find its focal length when immersed in water (n_water=1.33).
questions.explanation: Using the lensmaker's equation ratio: f_water/f_air = [(n_lens−1)/(n_lens/n_water−1)] × ... working through gives f_water ≈ 130cm — immersion in a denser medium significantly increases a lens's focal length.

questions.prompt: Consider an object placed 20cm from an achromatic doublet objective lens, forming a real image 30cm from the lens. If the dispersive powers of the two component glasses are in the ratio 2:3, compute the focal lengths of the individual lenses.
questions.explanation: Combined focal length from the lens equation (u = 20, v = 30): 1/f = 1/20 + 1/30 = 1/12, so f = 12 cm. For an achromatic doublet ω₁/f₁ + ω₂/f₂ = 0, so with ω₁:ω₂ = 2:3, f₂ = −1.5 f₁. Then 1/f₁ − 1/(1.5 f₁) = 1/(3 f₁) = 1/12 gives f₁ = 4 cm and f₂ = −6 cm.

questions.prompt: A plano-convex lens of refractive index 1.50 forms a virtual image with a magnification of 6. If the image is 12cm from the lens, calculate the radius of curvature of the curved surface.
questions.explanation: For a virtual image, magnification m=6 means v=−12cm, u=v/m=−2cm. Using 1/f=1/v−1/u and the lensmaker's equation 1/f=(n−1)/R for a plano-convex lens gives R ≈ 1.2cm.

questions.prompt: If the focal length of a converging lens is f, what is the nature of the image produced for an object placed beyond 2f?
options: Magnified, inverted, farther from the lens than the object
Diminished, inverted, closer to the lens than the object
questions.explanation: For an object beyond 2f, a converging lens produces a real, inverted, diminished image located between f and 2f on the other side — closer to the lens than the object itself.

questions.prompt: An object is placed 60cm from a converging lens of focal length 20cm. Calculate the position of the image formed.

Which of the following statements is/are true? (i) Optical density relates to how much a medium slows the transmission of light. (ii) During reflection, energy is not conserved. (iii) At a boundary that is a perfect reflector, there is no refraction.
questions.explanation: Optical density (i) correctly describes how a medium slows light. A perfect reflector (iii) correctly has no refraction, since all light reflects. Statement (ii) is false — reflection conserves energy (the light isn't lost, just redirected).

questions.prompt: The refractive index of water relative to air is 1.55, and that of oil relative to air is 1.73. Calculate the refractive index of water with respect to oil.
questions.explanation: n(water/oil) = n(water/air) ÷ n(oil/air) = 1.55/1.73 ≈ 0.90.

questions.prompt: The image of a pin formed by a diverging lens of focal length 12cm is 5cm from the lens (virtual, same side as the object). Calculate the distance of the pin from the lens.
questions.explanation: For a diverging lens, f=−12cm, and the virtual image is at v=−5cm. From 1/v=1/f−1/u: 1/u=1/f−1/v=1/(−12)−1/(−5)=−1/12+1/5=7/60, so u≈8.57cm.
questions.source: PHY104 2023/2024 (compendium, verified answer key) — corrects an earlier flagged question

questions.prompt: When a person uses a convex lens as a simple magnifying glass, the object must be placed at a distance:
options: More than one focal length but less than two
More than twice the focal length
questions.explanation: A magnifying glass works by producing a virtual, erect, magnified image — this only happens when the object is placed inside the focal length (u<f) of a converging lens.

questions.prompt: To read a book 20cm away, a man requires a lens of focal length 22cm (image formed at his near point). What is his natural near point (distance of distinct vision)?
If an object is placed in front of a converging lens such that its distance from the lens is thrice the focal length, determine the location of the image (in terms of the focal length).
A ray of light travelling in a liquid has an angle of incidence of 40.0°. What angle does the refracted ray in air make with the normal, if the critical angle at the liquid-air interface is 52.7°?
questions.explanation: Since n = 1/sin(critical angle), we get n = 1/sin(52.7°) ≈ 1.259. Applying Snell's law: sin(θ_air) = n×sin(40°) ≈ 1.259×0.643 ≈ 0.809, θ_air ≈ 54.1°.

questions.prompt: Which pair best illustrates an eye defect and the type of lens used to correct it?
questions.explanation: Hypermetropia (long-sightedness/far-sightedness) means the eye can't focus on near objects — a converging (convex) lens corrects this by adding extra converging power. (Myopia/short-sightedness needs the opposite: a diverging lens.)

questions.prompt: A girl who is near-sighted cannot see objects clearly beyond 25cm. If she has no astigmatism, calculate the power of the corrective contact lens prescribed so she can see clearly at infinity.
questions.explanation: A near-sighted (myopic) person's far point is at 25cm. The corrective lens must make an object at infinity appear to be at that far point: P = 1/f = 1/(−0.25m) = −4 diopters.

questions.prompt: If the focal length of a converging lens is f, what is the nature of the image produced for an object placed beyond 2f?
options: Diminished, inverted and closer to the lens than the object
Magnified, inverted and farther from the lens than the object
questions.explanation: For an object beyond 2f, a converging lens forms a real, inverted, diminished image located between f and 2f — closer to the lens than the object.

questions.prompt: A diver is 3.5m beneath the surface of still water (n=1.33). At what angle to the normal must the diver shine a beam of light towards the surface for it to just emerge?
questions.explanation: Light can only escape at or below the critical angle: θ_c=sin⁻¹(1/n)=sin⁻¹(1/1.33)≈48.8°.

questions.prompt: When a human eye with a power of +60D is fitted with a contact lens of −10D, what is the resulting combination?
questions.explanation: Combined power = 60+(−10)=50D. Since power is positive, the combination is converging. Focal length = 1/P = 1/50 = 0.02m = 2cm.

questions.prompt: A certain glass prism has a refractive index of 1.61 for red light and 1.66 for violet light. Light is incident symmetrically on the prism face at apex angle 60°. Find the difference in angles of deviation between the two colours.
questions.explanation: Using the minimum-deviation prism formula for each refractive index and taking the difference in resulting deviation angles gives approximately 5°.

questions.prompt: What is the length of a terrestrial telescope made of an objective lens of focal length 0.5m, a tube length of 0.4m, and an eyepiece of focal length 6cm?
questions.explanation: A terrestrial telescope's total length combines the objective focal length, the erecting tube length, and the eyepiece focal length: 50cm+? — working through the standard construction gives ≈56cm total.
questions.reviewNote: The key (56 cm) is just objective + eyepiece (50 + 6). The question also gives a 0.4 m tube length, and a terrestrial telescope's length normally includes the erecting section (50 + 40 + 6 = 96 cm, which is not an option). The data and key do not agree. Held back until the original is checked.

questions.prompt: A thin glass prism has a refracting angle of 20° (n_violet=1.6434, n_red=1.6648). Calculate the angle of dispersion produced.
questions.explanation: For a thin prism, deviation ≈ (n−1)×A. Dispersion = difference in deviation between colours = (n_red−n_violet)×A = (1.6648−1.6434)×20° ≈ 0.43°.

questions.prompt: The critical angle for light passing from a material of refractive index n₁=1.89 to a material of refractive index n₂=1.33 is:
Find the apparent depth of the bottom of a swimming pool as viewed from directly above, if the true depth is 1.6m. (n_water=1.33)
questions.explanation: Apparent depth = true depth/n = 1.6/1.33 ≈ 1.2m.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements is/are correct about light that is refracted? (i) The speed is unchanged. (ii) The frequency remains constant. (iii) The wavelength remains constant.
questions.explanation: When light refracts, only frequency stays constant (it's set by the source). Both speed AND wavelength change together (since v=fλ and f is fixed, v and λ must change proportionally) — so only statement (ii) is correct.

questions.prompt: When the frequency of the driving force of a system coincides with the natural undamped oscillating frequency of the system, which phenomenon is most likely to occur?
questions.explanation: Resonance occurs precisely when a driving force's frequency matches a system's natural frequency, causing the amplitude of oscillation to grow dramatically.

questions.prompt: The bonnet of a car is pushed down and it does not bounce up and down at all — instead it eases back to position. The shock absorbers are said to be:
questions.explanation: A system that returns to equilibrium without any oscillation, but more slowly than the critically-damped case, is overdamped. (Critically damped returns as fast as possible without any overshoot; underdamped oscillates before settling.)

questions.prompt: The equation of a damped oscillation is given as 3ẍ + 12ẋ + 39x = 0. What is the nature of the damping?
questions.explanation: Comparing to mẍ+bẋ+kx=0: m=3, b=12, k=39. Critical damping occurs when b²=4mk. Here b²=144, 4mk=468. Since b²<4mk, the system is underdamped (oscillates with decaying amplitude).

questions.prompt: The equation of motion for a harmonic oscillator is given as d²x/dt² = −16x. What type of oscillation is this, and what is its period?
questions.explanation: d²x/dt² = −16x is the SHM form a = −ω²x with ω² = 16, so ω = 4 rad/s and T = 2π/4 ≈ 1.57 s. There is no damping or driving term, so it is simple harmonic motion.
questions.sourceNote: Options and key corrected against the original paper (an earlier version had reconstructed options).

questions.prompt: The equation of motion for a point mass is given by 2ẍ + 3ẋ + 5x = 12sin(20t+φ). Calculate its natural (resonance) angular frequency.
questions.explanation: Natural frequency ω₀=√(k/m)=√(5/2)≈1.58 rad/s.

questions.prompt: The equation of motion for a point mass is given by 2ẍ + 3ẋ + 7x = 4cos(ωt+φ). What is the value of ω for maximum displacement amplitude of the particle?
questions.explanation: The amplitude-resonance frequency accounts for damping: ω_res=√(k/m − b²/(2m²)) = √(7/2 − 3²/8) ≈ 1.54 rad/s.

questions.prompt: The various methods of describing a damped oscillator include all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Decrement, relaxation time, modulus of damping, and quality factor are all standard, established ways to characterize damped oscillations — none of them is actually excluded, so 'None of the above' is correct.
questions.sourceNote: Options and key corrected against the original paper (an earlier version had reconstructed options).

questions.prompt: A simple pendulum of amplitude 0.05m is set into oscillation. After 5 minutes its amplitude has fallen to 0.025m. Calculate the relaxation time of the oscillation.
questions.explanation: Amplitude decays as A=A₀e^(−t/τ). Setting A/A₀=0.5 at t=300s: 0.5=e^(−300/τ) → τ=300/ln(2)≈432.9s.

questions.prompt: The equation of motion for a point mass is given by 3ẍ + 7ẋ + 10x = 10sin(20t+φ). Find the mechanical impedance per unit mass.
questions.explanation: Mechanical impedance per unit mass at driving frequency ω=20: Z/m = √((k/m−ω²)²·(m/ω)² + b²)/m — working through with m=3,b=7,k=10,ω=20 gives ≈19.97 Ω/kg.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements is/are correct? (i) The damping force is conservative. (ii) The damping force is non-conservative. (iii) The damping force is both conservative and non-conservative.
questions.explanation: Damping forces (like friction or air resistance) always dissipate energy as heat rather than storing and returning it — this is the definition of a non-conservative force. Only statement (ii) is correct.

questions.prompt: The equation of a damped harmonic oscillator is given as x = x₀e^(−0.4t)cos(ωt). What type of oscillation is this?
questions.explanation: The presence of a cos(ωt) term with a slowly-decaying exponential envelope (small decay constant 0.4) indicates the system still oscillates many times before dying out — this is lightly (under)damped behavior.

questions.prompt: When the frequency of the driving force of a system coincides with the natural undamped oscillating frequency of the system, which phenomenon is most likely to occur?
questions.explanation: Resonance occurs precisely when a driving force's frequency matches a system's natural frequency, causing amplitude to build dramatically.

questions.prompt: The equation of motion for a point mass is given by 3ẍ + 6ẋ + 14x = 120cos(20t+φ). Determine the angular frequency of the driving force.
questions.explanation: The driving frequency is simply the coefficient of t inside the cosine term: ω=20 rad/s (this is given directly, not something to derive from m, b, k).

questions.prompt: The bonnet of a car is pushed down and does not bounce up and down at all — instead it sinks back slowly. The shock absorbers are said to be:
questions.explanation: Returning to equilibrium without any oscillation, but sluggishly rather than as fast as possible, describes an overdamped system.

questions.prompt: Determine the resonance (angular) frequency for the equation of motion 5ẍ + 7ẋ + 9x = 8sin(πt).
questions.explanation: Amplitude-resonance frequency with damping: ω_res = √(k/m − b²/(2m²)) = √(9/5 − 49/50) = √0.82 = 0.91 rad/s.

questions.prompt: Find the particle velocity at t=0 for the equation of motion x = 5e^(−0.75t)sin(ωt), where ω=4 rad/s.
